before.name: the plan
before.label: before the essay
before.text: The company he left ran on his instructions for eighty years without the judgment that wrote them. It gave the United States its eyes over the Soviet Union, put the first photograph of the Earth in front of humanity, and then, in a single year, 1976, invented the digital image, patented the color filter every phone sensor now uses, licensed it out to the world, and chose to collect rent instead of build. It ended as the man it began by firing: **George Selden**, the patent attorney Eastman let go in 1887 for being a man who held paper rather than made things, who then kept a gasoline-engine application alive for sixteen years by amendment and collected a fee on every automobile built in America until Henry Ford broke him in court in 1911. On October 23, 2012, the last roll came off a machine that had run a hundred and one years. Two months later the arsenal built to cover every avenue was sold for a fifth of asking to Apple and Google, which had inherited the position Kodak held for a century. **Kodak was the Apple and Google of its day, and it was liquidated into them.**

before.name: the outline
before.label: before the essay
before.text: The received story is not stupid. It is incomplete, which is worse, because incomplete stories are the ones that stick. Film margins were extraordinary and every digital move was self-harm on the balance sheet, so renting rather than building was defensible for about twenty years. What the slide leaves out is that Kodak owned the future it declined to build, and that the decision was a decision. In 1879 a Rochester patent attorney named George Selden filed an application for a gasoline road engine, and his client George Eastman signed it as a witness. Selden kept that application alive for sixteen years by amendment, then collected a fee on nearly every automobile built in America until Henry Ford beat him in court in 1911. He made nothing and owned everything. A century later, Eastman's company was doing the same thing.
